analysis.one_liner: Ends dozens of tax breaks for oil, gas, coal, fund managers, agribusiness, and high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal a long list of special tax breaks written into the tax code: preferences for oil and gas producers and coal companies, the carried-interest break that lets investment fund managers pay capital-gains rates on their pay, agribusiness and timber breaks, generous inventory accounting rules for large companies, limits on itemized deductions for the highest earners, and several international tax preferences. It would also phase out health savings account deductions and the foreign earned income exclusion, and replace the tax-exempt status of municipal bonds with a direct federal subsidy to issuers.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal treasury, which would collect more revenue from industries and households now using these tax breaks; ordinary taxpayers to the extent the revenue is used to lower deficits or fund services; and fund investors and workers whose tax bills are not lowered by these preferences.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the major oil and gas tax preferences, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, the marginal well credit, the intangible drilling costs deduction, percentage depletion, and the domestic manufacturing deduction for oil and gas [S2][S3].
Repeals coal, lignite, and oil shale preferences, including the capital-gains treatment of coal royalties and percentage depletion [S2][S3].

Treats income of investment fund managers from their partnership interests as ordinary income rather than capital gains, closing the carried-interest break, and taxes transferred service partnership interests at value [S2][S3].
Limits the benefit of itemized deductions to the 28-percent bracket for taxpayers with income over $200,000 ($250,000 joint), so high earners no longer get outsized benefit from deductions [S3].
Repeals the last-in, first-out and lower-of-cost-or-market inventory accounting methods and eliminates the meal and entertainment expense deduction [S2][S3].

Eliminates agribusiness and timber tax expenditures, including expensing of fertilizer and multi-period production costs, capital-gains treatment of timber sales, and the race horse depreciation break [S2][S3].

Raises taxes on international income shifting, including excess income from transfers of intangibles to low-taxed foreign affiliates and interest deductions allocated to deferred foreign income [S2][S3].
Converts the tax exemption for state and local bonds into a direct federal subsidy paid to issuers, replacing a break that mainly benefits high-bracket bondholders [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, coal companies, investment fund managers taking carried interest, agribusiness and timber owners, large inventory-heavy businesses, multinational corporations using deferral and income shifting, high-income itemizers, Americans working abroad who lose the foreign earned income exclusion, and HSA and Archer MSA holders who lose the deduction.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel, finance, agribusiness, multinationals, high earners

drawbacks.text: The bill phases out health savings accounts and Archer medical savings accounts, ending the tax deduction for contributions, which reduces a savings vehicle used by middle-class families paying health costs [S2][S3].
It repeals the foreign earned income exclusion, raising income taxes on American citizens working and living abroad [S3].

Closing oil, gas, and coal tax preferences would raise production costs for those industries, which could be passed to consumers through energy prices and could reduce domestic exploration incentives [S3].
Ending tax-exempt municipal bonds could raise borrowing costs for state and local governments, though the bill substitutes a direct federal subsidy at a 28-percent rate to issuers instead [S3].

Repealing LIFO inventory accounting would trigger large one-time income recognition for retailers, refiners, and other inventory-heavy businesses, spread over eight years, with costs potentially passed to consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's weight falls clearly on concentrated interests: fossil fuel producers, fund managers, multinationals, and high-income filers. Its main cost to ordinary people is narrow — the HSA phase-out and the foreign earned income exclusion touch middle-class households directly, and energy or consumer prices could rise at the margin. The municipal bond swap is designed to keep public borrowing functioning while redirecting the benefit from bondholders to issuers. On balance the bill is a straightforward revenue-raising, loophole-closing measure, though the HSA repeal is a real cost to families who use those accounts.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative John Tierney of Massachusetts and four Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on July 11, 2011 [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, coal companies, investment fund managers claiming carried interest at capital-gains rates, agribusiness and timber interests, multinational corporations using deferral, and high-income itemizers all kept their existing tax breaks because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel, coal, fund manager, agribusiness tax-break users

for.name: Rep. John F. Tierney
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate dozens of tax expenditures and referred it to his own committee.

for.name: Reps. Keith Ellison, Raul Grijalva, Jesse Jackson Jr., and Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other members signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action on the bill; there were no floor votes.

industries.note: The bill terminates the enhanced oil recovery credit, marginal well credit, intangible drilling cost deduction, percentage depletion, and the domestic manufacturing deduction for oil and gas. These breaks lower the effective tax rate on one of the most profitable industries, a cost borne by other taxpayers [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Coal, lignite, and oil shale companies
industries.note: The bill ends development and exploration deductions, percentage depletion, the domestic production deduction, and capital-gains treatment of coal royalties. The revenue cost of these breaks otherwise falls on ordinary taxpayers [S2][S3].

The bill taxes investment managers' partnership income as ordinary wages rather than capital gains, ending a break worth billions to the wealthiest fund managers that ordinary wage earners cannot use [S2][S3].

The bill eliminates expensing for fertilizer and multi-period livestock and crop costs, capital-gains treatment of timber sales, reforestation amortization, and the race horse depreciation break [S2][S3].

The bill limits interest deductions tied to deferred foreign income, taxes excess income from intangible transfers to low-taxed affiliates, and tightens foreign tax credit rules, raising taxes on income shifted abroad [S2][S3].
Repealing LIFO and lower-of-cost-or-market accounting would raise taxable income, with any one-time adjustment collected over eight years [S3].

industries.industry: Municipal bond market and state/local issuers
industries.note: The bill ends federal tax exemption for new state and local bonds but replaces it with a direct Treasury subsidy to issuers, aiming to preserve public borrowing while shifting the benefit from high-bracket bondholders to governments [S3].
The bill phases out the HSA deduction, reducing the tax advantage of these accounts, though the accounts themselves would retain tax treatment for two years [S3].
